title: Records and Pattern Matching
description: Learn how C# records provide built-in immutability and value-based equality, and how pattern matching with switch expressions replaces verbose if/else chains with clean, expressive syntax.

data.text: **Records** (introduced in C# 9) and **pattern matching** (evolved across C# 7 through C# 11) are modern C# features designed to make data-centric code cleaner, safer, and more expressive. Records give you immutable data with value-based equality out of the box, while pattern matching lets you write complex conditional logic that reads like plain English.

A **record** is a reference type optimized for storing data. Unlike classes, which focus on encapsulation and behavior, records focus on what the data *is*. When you define a record, C# automatically generates: a constructor, property initializers, `ToString()`, `GetHashCode()`, and `Equals()` — all based on the properties you declare. Records are **immutable by default**, meaning properties cannot change after creation.

terms.definition: A C# reference type (C# 9+) designed for immutable data with value-based equality.
A record declared with constructor parameters in parentheses: public record Person(string Name).
Two records are equal if their property values are equal, not just if they reference the same memory.
Creates a copy of a record with specified properties changed: person with { Age = 30 }.
A language feature that tests values against shapes, types, or conditions using a concise syntax.
A concise expression (not statement) that returns a value based on matching patterns.

data.text: There are two ways to define a record: **positional** (compact, with constructor parameters) and **standard** (with explicit property declarations inside curly braces). Positional records are great for simple data carriers, while standard records give you more control over mutability and additional logic.

data.content: Declare a record with constructor parameters — C# generates init-only properties automatically.

data.title: Standard Record with Mutable Properties
data.content: Use standard record syntax when you need init-only or mutable properties, validation, or additional members.

data.text: This is one of the most important differences between records and classes. With a **class**, two objects are equal only if they point to the same memory location (`ReferenceEquals`). With a **record**, two separate instances are equal if all their properties have the same values. This mirrors how we think about data — two people named "Alice Johnson" with the same age are the same person *for data purposes*, even if they are different objects in memory.

data.title: Value-Based Equality in Practice
data.content: Records compare by value; classes compare by reference.

data.text: Pattern matching lets you test a value against a **pattern** — a shape, type, range, or condition — and extract information if it matches. It replaces messy nested if/else chains with code that reads naturally. C# has expanded pattern matching dramatically since C# 7, adding type patterns, relational patterns, logical patterns, and property patterns.

data.title: Type Pattern Matching
data.content: Use case labels with type patterns to branch based on the runtime type of an object.

data.text: A **switch expression** is a concise, expression-based alternative to the switch statement. It returns a value directly instead of executing statements in each case. The `switch` keyword comes after the expression being evaluated, and `case` clauses use the arrow `=>` syntax.

data.content: Convert a numeric score to a letter grade using a clean switch expression.

data.text: Property patterns let you match against specific property values inside an object. This is especially powerful with records because records are designed around their data shape. You can nest patterns to match deeply nested structures cleanly.

data.content: Match on record properties using nested property patterns.

data.text: C# 11 introduced **list patterns**, which let you match against the shape of arrays or lists directly in a pattern. You can check the length and even match specific elements at specific positions using the slice operator `..`.

data.title: When to Use Records
data.text: Use records for data-centric types: DTOs, configuration objects, API responses, and domain entities where identity comes from values. Use classes for objects with significant behavior or mutable state managed by methods.

items.text: Use positional record syntax for simple data carriers
items.hint: public record Name(Type Prop1, Type Prop2)

items.text: Use standard record syntax when you need validation or extra members
items.hint: public record Name { public Type Prop { get; init; } }

items.text: Use 'with' expressions instead of modifying records directly
items.hint: var copy = original with { Prop = newValue }

items.text: Prefer switch expressions over switch statements when returning a value
Use relational patterns (>=, <) for numeric range matching
Use logical patterns (and, or, not) to combine conditions

data.title: Build a Shape Calculator with Records and Pattern Matching
data.description: Create a simple shape hierarchy using records and a pattern-matching switch expression to calculate area.
steps: Define a Shape record with a Name property.
Define Circle, Rectangle, and Triangle as record types that inherit from Shape with their own properties.
Write a CalculateArea(Shape shape) method that uses a switch expression to dispatch to the correct area formula.
Create an array of Shape instances and iterate over them, printing each shape's name and calculated area.
Bonus: Add a with expression to create a larger version of a shape.
data.expectedOutcome: A working shape system demonstrating record inheritance, positional parameters, and switch expression pattern matching.

items.question: Are records really immutable?
items.answer: Positional records create init-only properties, so they cannot change after construction. Standard records can include mutable properties if you explicitly use get; set;. Records are immutable by convention and default, not by absolute enforcement.

items.question: Can records inherit from classes or other records?
items.answer: Records can inherit from other records. A record inheriting from another record must call the base constructor explicitly. Records cannot inherit from classes, and classes cannot inherit from records.

items.question: What is the difference between a switch expression and a switch statement?
items.answer: A switch statement executes code blocks (with break/return). A switch expression returns a value and uses => for each arm. Switch expressions are preferred when you want a result from the match.

items.question: When should I use a when filter in a case clause?
items.answer: Use when when a single type or value needs additional conditions. For example: case int i when i > 100. For combined conditions on the same value, prefer relational and logical patterns inside a switch expression.

items.question: What C# version introduced list patterns?
items.answer: List patterns were introduced in C# 11 (.NET 7). They let you match arrays and lists by length and element values directly in the pattern syntax.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Records are immutable data types with value-based equality
Positional syntax is concise for simple data carriers
'with' creates a modified copy without changing the original
Switch expressions replace verbose if/else chains
Type patterns match runtime types and cast automatically
Relational and logical patterns express ranges and combined conditions
Property patterns match against object properties
data.takeaway: Records and pattern matching let you write data-focused, expressive C# code that is safer and easier to read than equivalent class-based code with manual equality and nested conditionals.
